title: Seven days of silence (Job 2:11–13)
hookLine: his friends sit with him for a week without speaking; that's the best thing they do
last: THE LORD GAVE, THE LORD TOOK.

cards: The funeral home. The hospital corridor. The kitchen of a friend whose marriage just ended.
Someone walks in with a casserole or a card, mind racing for the right thing to say, and everything sounds wrong. They're in a better place. It'll get easier.
Everything happens for a reason. A mouth opens, and closes again. The silence is hard to bear, and it's tempting to fill it with something.
Three men in the book of Job, at least at first, did something braver. They said nothing at all. For a week.

teach.b: The King James Bible: "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him."
They made an appointment. They coordinated, traveled from three different places, and arrived together, on purpose.

Then they see him from a distance and don't recognize him; disease and grief have changed him that much. They weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust into the air over their heads, the signs of mourning.
And then: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." On the ground, in the ash, at his level.
Seven days of mourning appears elsewhere in the Bible too: Joseph mourned his father Jacob for seven days.
Jews still keep that week of sitting with mourners, called shiva, from the Hebrew for seven. Then a quiet detail: the friends don't speak until Job speaks first. They follow his lead.

teach.h: FOR THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.
teach.b: The sad part, as the next days will show, is that once they open their mouths, it goes badly. Some readers say the week of silence was the best comfort they gave.
Paul's letter to the Romans puts the same instinct simply: "weep with them that weep."

how: Christians practice a ministry of presence by visiting the sick and the grieving, staying at wakes and sitting with the dying; many pastors and hospital chaplains point to Job's friends' silent week as a model.

games.q: your friend has lost his children, his health and everything he owned. you've traveled to see him and you barely recognize him. what do you do?
o: sit on the ground beside him and say nothing.
tell him it could have been worse.
games.why: "so they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him." some readers call it the best thing they did.

practice: Picture someone near you who is hurting, and imagine sitting down beside them, on the floor if that's where they are. Notice the urge to say something helpful, and let it rise and fall without acting on it.
If you pray, hold them before God without words; if not, simply keep them company in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Shiva. The Hebrew word for seven, the mourning week Job's three friends kept, sitting on the ground with him, not one of them speaking.

orig.note: Hebrew: seven days. the root of shiva, the Jewish week of mourning.
